title: Operator domains, deficiency spaces and boundary realizations

items.title: Closed symmetric operators and deficiency data
items.design_state: Assigned design item; complete current statement and argument are recorded in its item carrier.
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert
space and let $S:D(S)\to H$ be a densely defined, closed, symmetric linear
operator. The domain $D(S)$ is part of the operator data. Its adjoint is the
operator $S^*:D(S^*)\to H$ characterized by
$\langle Sf,g\rangle=\langle f,S^*g\rangle$ for every $f\in D(S)$ and
$g\in D(S^*)$, using an inner product linear in its first argument. A **graph
core** for $S$ is a linear subspace $C\subseteq D(S)$ dense for the graph norm
$\|f\|_S=(\|f\|^2+\|Sf\|^2)^{1/2}$; equivalently, the graph of the restriction
$S|_C$ is dense in the graph of $S$.

Fix a positive scalar $E_*$ and write $I_H$ for the identity on $H$. The
**scaled deficiency subspaces** of $S$ at $E_*$ are
$N_+(S;E_*):=\ker(S^*-iE_*I_H)$ and
$N_-(S;E_*):=\ker(S^*+iE_*I_H)$. Their **deficiency indices** are
$n_\pm(S;E_*):=\dim N_\pm(S;E_*)$, where Hilbert dimension means the
cardinality of an orthonormal basis as in the standard deficiency-index
definition. The spaces are closed: if $g_k\in N_\pm(S;E_*)$ and $g_k\to g$,
then $S^*g_k=\pm iE_*g_k\to\pm iE_*g$, so closedness of $S^*$ gives
$g\in D(S^*)$ and $S^*g=\pm iE_*g$. The dimension convention is well defined
under Choice by the cited deficiency-index definition.

For any specified linear trace map $\gamma:D(S^*)\to B$ into a vector space
$B$ and specified linear subspace $\Lambda\subseteq B$, the restriction of
$S^*$ to $\{f\in D(S^*):\gamma(f)\in\Lambda\}$ is the boundary realization
specified by $(\gamma,\Lambda)$. Its domain and trace data are part of the
operator realization; the differential expression alone is not.
items.proof_route: Define kernels and prove their closedness using closedness of S*; explain E* nondimensionalization.

items.title: Minimal and maximal domains of the interval Laplacian
items.design_state: Scaffolder-added local supplier; complete proof authored in this batch.
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice, Countable Choice, and Dependent Choice. Let
$0<L<\infty$, let $H=L^2(0,L;\mathbb C)$, and use the spaces $H^1(0,L)$ and
$H^2(0,L)$ and their continuous endpoint traces defined by the one-dimensional
Sobolev suppliers. Define $T_c f=-D^2f$ on $D(T_c)=C_c^\infty(0,L)$. Then
$T_c$ is densely defined and symmetric, its adjoint is
$T_{\max}f=-D^2f$ on exactly $D(T_{\max})=H^2(0,L)$, and its closure
$T_{\min}=\overline{T_c}=T_c^{**}$ has domain
$$D(T_{\min})=\{f\in H^2(0,L): f(0)=f'(0)=f(L)=f'(L)=0\},$$
with $T_{\min}f=-D^2f$. The trace map
$\gamma:H^2(0,L)\to\mathbb C^4$ defined by
$\gamma(f)=(f(0),f(L),f'(0),f'(L))$ is surjective.
items.proof_route: Identify the adjoint distributionally, prove an L² second derivative forces H² regularity by integrating twice, prescribe four traces with Hermite cubics, and characterize the double-adjoint domain by Green’s identity and trace surjectivity.

references.title: Gerald Teschl, Mathematical Methods in Quantum Mechanics, 1st edition 2009
references.locator: Section 9.1, Lemma 9.4 and regular-endpoint example, printed pp.184–185

references.title: Manuel Asorey, Alberto Ibort, and Giuseppe Marmo, Global Theory of Quantum Boundary Conditions and Topology Change
references.locator: Section 2, printed pp.4–6; Appendix A, printed p.20: interval Laplacian domain and boundary data

items.strategy:
**Given:** The hypotheses and objects in the Statement.

1.1 Density follows from [F3]. For $f,g\in C_c^\infty(0,L)$, integration by
parts gives $\langle -f'',g\rangle=\langle f,-g''\rangle$, since both
functions and their derivatives vanish near the endpoints. Thus $T_c$ is
dense and symmetric. [A1, F2, F3]

1.2 Suppose $u\in L^2(0,L)$ has distributional second derivative
$D^2u=h\in L^2(0,L)$. By [F6], $h\in L^1(0,L)$. Define
$v(x)=\int_0^x h(t)\,dt$. Then $|v(x)|\le\|h\|_{L^1}\le\sqrt L\|h\|_2$,
so $v\in L^2(0,L)$. For every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(0,L)$, Fubini applies
because $\int_0^L\int_0^x|h(t)||\varphi'(x)|\,dt\,dx\le
\|h\|_1\|\varphi'\|_1<\infty$, and [F7] gives
$$\int_0^L v(x)\varphi'(x)\,dx=\int_0^Lh(t)\left(\int_t^L\varphi'(x)\,dx\right)dt=-\int_0^Lh(t)\varphi(t)\,dt,$$
because [F7], applied to real and imaginary parts, gives
$\int_t^L\varphi'(x)\,dx=\varphi(L)-\varphi(t)=-\varphi(t)$ since
$\varphi$ vanishes near $L$. Hence $Dv=h$ weakly and $v\in H^1$.
The distribution $Du-v$ has derivative zero. For every test function
$\varphi$ of integral zero, its primitive
$\psi(x)=\int_0^x\varphi(t)\,dt$ is compactly supported in $(0,L)$, and hence
$(Du-v)(\varphi)=(Du-v)(D\psi)=-(D(Du-v))(\psi)=0$. Obtain a test
function $\eta$ with integral one as follows. The constant function $1$ lies
in $L^2(0,L)$ with norm $\sqrt L$. By the density in [F3], choose
$\chi\in C_c^\infty(0,L)$ with $\|\chi-1\|_2<\sqrt L/2$; then
$\|\chi\|_2>\sqrt L/2$. Set $\eta=|\chi|^2/\|\chi\|_2^2$. It is a smooth
compactly supported test function and $\int_0^L\eta=1$. For arbitrary
$\varphi$,
$\varphi-(\int_0^L\varphi)\eta$ has integral zero, so
$(Du-v)(\varphi)=(Du-v)(\eta)\int_0^L\varphi$. Therefore $Du-v$ is a constant
distribution, $Du=v+c\in L^2$, and $u\in H^2(0,L)$ by [F1].
[A1, F1, F3, F6, F7]

1.3 The Hermite cubic polynomials
$h_{00}(s)=2s^3-3s^2+1$,
$h_{01}(s)=-2s^3+3s^2$,
$h_{10}(s)=s^3-2s^2+s$, and
$h_{11}(s)=s^3-s^2$ satisfy
the endpoint data
$(h_{00}(0),h_{00}(1),h_{00}'(0),h_{00}'(1))=(1,0,0,0)$,
$(h_{01}(0),h_{01}(1),h_{01}'(0),h_{01}'(1))=(0,1,0,0)$,
$(h_{10}(0),h_{10}(1),h_{10}'(0),h_{10}'(1))=(0,0,1,0)$, and
$(h_{11}(0),h_{11}(1),h_{11}'(0),h_{11}'(1))=(0,0,0,1)$.
Consequently, for arbitrary
$a_0,a_L,d_0,d_L\in\mathbb C$, the polynomial
$p(x)=a_0h_{00}(x/L)+a_Lh_{01}(x/L)
+Ld_0h_{10}(x/L)+Ld_Lh_{11}(x/L)$ has
$p(0)=a_0$, $p(L)=a_L$, $p'(0)=d_0$, and $p'(L)=d_L$. It belongs to
$H^2(0,L)$, proving that $\gamma$ is onto. [F1, construct, algebra]

2.1 If $g\in H^2(0,L)$, [F2] applied with a compactly supported test function
shows $\langle T_cf,g\rangle=\langle f,-D^2g\rangle$; thus
$g\in D(T_c^*)$ and $T_c^*g=-D^2g$. Conversely, if $g\in D(T_c^*)$ and
$h=T_c^*g$, testing the adjoint identity against every
$f\in C_c^\infty(0,L)$ gives distributionally $D^2g=-h\in L^2$. Step 1.2
then gives $g\in H^2(0,L)$. Hence $T_c^*=T_{\max}$ with exactly the claimed
domain. [A1, F1, F2, F4, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 By [F5] and step 2.1, $T_{\min}=T_c^{**}=T_{\max}^*$. If
$u\in D(T_{\max}^*)$ and $h=T_{\max}^*u$, testing against
$C_c^\infty(0,L)\subset H^2(0,L)$ gives distributionally $D^2u=-h$.
Step 1.2 implies $u\in H^2(0,L)$. The adjoint identity for all
$g\in H^2(0,L)$ and [F2] now reads
$\langle\Gamma_1g,\Gamma_0u\rangle-\langle\Gamma_0g,\Gamma_1u\rangle=0$.
By step 1.3 the two traces of $g$ can be prescribed independently: first set
$\Gamma_0g=0$ and vary $\Gamma_1g$ to obtain $\Gamma_0u=0$; then set
$\Gamma_1g=0$ and vary $\Gamma_0g$ to obtain $\Gamma_1u=0$. Conversely, if
$u\in H^2$ has both traces zero, [F2] gives
$\langle T_{\max}g,u\rangle=\langle g,-D^2u\rangle$ for every
$g\in H^2$, so $u\in D(T_{\max}^*)$. Therefore
$D(T_{\min})=\{u\in H^2:\Gamma_0u=\Gamma_1u=0\}$ and its action is
$-D^2u$. [A1, F2, F5, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 1.3]

4.1 The preceding steps establish density, symmetry, the exact adjoint, the
closure domain, and trace surjectivity as stated. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 1.3, step 3.1] ∎

items.title: Unitary deficiency parameterization at a reference scale
items.design_state: Assigned design item; complete current statement and argument are recorded in its item carrier.
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert
space and $S:D(S)\to H$ a densely defined, closed, symmetric linear operator.
Fix $E_*>0$ and let $N_\pm=N_\pm(S;E_*)$ and
$n_\pm=\dim N_\pm$ be the scaled deficiency spaces and indices. For every
unitary map $V:N_+\to N_-$, the operator
$$D(S_V)=D(S)\oplus\{u+Vu:u\in N_+\},\qquad S_V(f+u+Vu)=Sf+iE_*u-iE_*Vu$$
is a self-adjoint extension of $S$. Every self-adjoint extension of $S$ is
uniquely $S_V$ for one such $V$. Consequently $S$ has a self-adjoint
extension if and only if $n_+=n_-$.
items.proof_route: Use the Cayley partial isometry, orthogonal range decompositions and graph-norm decomposition; check both adjoint inclusions, including infinite deficiency indices.

references.title: Gerald Teschl, Mathematical Methods in Quantum Mechanics, 1st edition 2009
Ovidiu Costin, Functional Analysis and Elements of Resurgence Theory

items.strategy:
**Given:** The objects in the Statement. Put $A=E_*^{-1}S$ on $D(A)=D(S)$.

1.1 The graph of $A$ is the image of the graph of $S$ under the bounded
invertible map $(f,g)\mapsto(f,E_*^{-1}g)$ on $H\oplus H$, so it is closed;
real scaling preserves symmetry. If $g\in D(S^*)$, then for every
$f\in D(S)$,
$\langle Af,g\rangle=E_*^{-1}\langle Sf,g\rangle
=\langle f,E_*^{-1}S^*g\rangle$, so $g\in D(A^*)$ and
$A^*g=E_*^{-1}S^*g$. Conversely, if $g\in D(A^*)$, then
$\langle Sf,g\rangle=E_*\langle Af,g\rangle
=\langle f,E_*A^*g\rangle$, so $g\in D(S^*)$ and
$S^*g=E_*A^*g$. Therefore $D(A^*)=D(S^*)$ and
$A^*=E_*^{-1}S^*$. Since
$A^*\mp iI=E_*^{-1}(S^*\mp iE_*I)$, the ordinary deficiency spaces of
$A$ at $\pm i$ are exactly $N_\pm$. [F1, F7, algebra]

1.2 Suppose $n_+=n_-$. Choose orthonormal bases $(e_j)_{j\in J_+}$ of $N_+$
and $(f_j)_{j\in J_-}$ of $N_-$. By [F6], choose a bijection
$\pi:J_+\to J_-$. The map $V_0e_j=f_{\pi(j)}$ preserves norms on finite
linear combinations by orthonormality, so it extends continuously to an
isometry $V:N_+\to N_-$. Its range contains the finite span of the $f_j$,
which is dense; the range of an isometry from the complete space $N_+$ is
closed, so $V$ is onto and unitary. [A1, F6, construct]

2.1 For $f\in D(A)$, symmetry makes $\langle Af,f\rangle$ real; expanding the
two norms gives
$\|(A\pm iI)f\|^2=\|Af\|^2+\|f\|^2$. Thus $A\pm iI$ are injective. If
$(A\pm iI)f_k$ converges, the norm identity applied to differences makes
$(f_k)$ Cauchy and then $(Af_k)$ Cauchy; closedness of $A$ shows the limit is
in the range. Hence $M_\pm:=\operatorname{ran}(A\pm iI)$ are closed. By [F2]
and [F3], $H=M_+\oplus N_+=M_-\oplus N_-$, with orthogonal sums.
[step 1.1, F2, F3]

2.2 Equip $D(A^*)$ with the graph inner product
$\langle f,g\rangle_{A^*}=\langle f,g\rangle+\langle A^*f,A^*g\rangle$.
It is complete by [F2, F4], and $D(A)$ is a closed subspace because $A$ is
closed and $A^*f=Af$ there. If $z\in D(A^*)$ is graph-orthogonal to $D(A)$,
then for every $f\in D(A)$,
$\langle Af,A^*z\rangle=-\langle f,z\rangle$. By the adjoint definition,
this means $A^*z\in D(A^*)$ and $A^{*2}z=-z$. Therefore
$z_+=(z-iA^*z)/2$ and $z_-=(z+iA^*z)/2$ satisfy
$A^*z_+=iz_+$ and $A^*z_-=-iz_-$, and $z=z_++z_-$. Conversely,
$D(A)$ is graph-orthogonal to both kernels: for $u\in N_+$,
$\langle f,u\rangle+\langle Af,A^*u\rangle
=\langle f,u\rangle+\langle Af,iu\rangle=0$ by the adjoint identity and
conjugate-linearity in the second argument, and the same computation with
$A^*u=-iu$ holds for $u\in N_-$. If $u\in N_+$ and $v\in N_-$, then
$\langle u,v\rangle+\langle A^*u,A^*v\rangle
=\langle u,v\rangle+\langle iu,-iv\rangle=0$. Thus the two kernels are
graph-orthogonal to each other. Applying [F3] in the graph Hilbert space proves the orthogonal
decomposition
$D(A^*)=D(A)\oplus N_+\oplus N_-$. [step 1.1, F2, F3, F4, F7]

3.1 Define $C_A:M_+\to M_-$ by
$C_A((A+iI)f)=(A-iI)f$. Injectivity of $A+iI$ makes this well defined, the
norm identity in step 2.1 makes it an isometry, and it is onto $M_-$. Define
$W(m+u)=C_Am-Vu$ for $m\in M_+$ and $u\in N_+$. The decompositions from
step 2.1 make $W$ well defined; it is unitary because its two orthogonal summands
are mapped isometrically onto $M_-$ and $N_-$. For $f\in D(A)$,
$(I-W)(A+iI)f=2if$, so $\operatorname{ran}(I-W)$ is dense. If $Wz=z$, then
$z$ is orthogonal to $\operatorname{ran}(I-W)$ by unitarity, hence to the
dense domain $D(A)$, so $z=0$. The Cayley correspondence [F5] therefore gives
a self-adjoint operator $A_V$ with Cayley transform $W$. [F2, F3, F5, step 2.1]

4.1 For $m=(A+iI)f$ and $u\in N_+$, direct calculation gives
$(I-W)(m+u)=2if+u+Vu$ and
$i(I+W)(m+u)=2iAf+iu-iVu$. The Cayley inverse is
$A_V=i(I+W)(I-W)^{-1}$ on $\operatorname{ran}(I-W)$, so
$D(A_V)=\operatorname{ran}(I-W)=D(A)+\{u+Vu:u\in N_+\}$ and
$A_V(2if+u+Vu)=2iAf+iu-iVu$. Equivalently, after renaming $2if$ as $f$,
$A_V(f+u+Vu)=Af+iu-iVu$. The sum is direct: if $f=u+Vu\in D(A)$, then
$(I-W)(A+iI)f=2if=(I-W)(2iu)$; injectivity of $I-W$ gives
$(A+iI)f=2iu$. Its left side lies in $M_+$ and its right side in $N_+$,
whose intersection is zero, so $u=f=0$. Multiplication by $E_*$ gives the
displayed domain and action for $S_V=E_*A_V$. The two-way scalar-adjoint
calculation in step 1.1 applies to $A_V$ as well, so
$S_V^*=E_*A_V^*=S_V$. Thus $S_V$ is a self-adjoint
extension of $S$. [F5, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

4.2 Conversely, let $T$ be any self-adjoint extension of $S$ and put
$R=E_*^{-1}T$. The two-way scalar-adjoint calculation in step 1.1 gives
$R^*=E_*^{-1}T^*=R$, so $R$ is a self-adjoint extension of $A$. Its Cayley transform $C_R$
is unitary by [F5] and agrees with $C_A$ on $M_+$, since $R$ equals $A$ on
$D(A)$. A unitary carrying $M_+$ onto $M_-$ carries their orthogonal
complements $N_+$ onto $N_-$ by step 2.1 and [F2]; hence
$C_R(N_+)=N_-$. Put $V=-C_R|_{N_+}$; this is unitary. The
unitary $W$ constructed from this $V$ agrees with $C_R$ on both orthogonal
summands of $H$, so uniqueness in [F5] gives $R=A_V$. This determines $V$
uniquely from $T$ and proves that every self-adjoint extension of $S$ is
uniquely $S_V$. [F2, F5, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1]

5.1 If $n_+=n_-$, step 1.2 supplies a unitary and step 4.1 supplies a
self-adjoint extension. If an extension exists, step 4.2 supplies a unitary
$N_+\to N_-$, so its orthonormal bases have bijective index sets and
$n_+=n_-$. This proves the existence equivalence and the complete
parameterization. [A1, F6, step 1.2, step 4.1, step 4.2] ∎

items.title: All self-adjoint interval Laplacian boundary conditions
items.design_state: Assigned design item; complete current statement and argument are recorded in its item carrier.
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice, Countable Choice, and Dependent Choice. Let
$0<L<\infty$, let $H=L^2(0,L;\mathbb C)$, and let $T_{\min}$ and
$T_{\max}=T_{\min}^*$ be the minimal and maximal realizations of
$-D^2$ from the preceding interval-domain lemma. Fix a positive reference
length $\ell$. For $f\in H^2(0,L)$ define
$\Gamma_0f=(f(0),f(L))$ and
$\Gamma_1f=(f'(0),-f'(L))$. Let
$U(2)=\{U\in M_2(\mathbb C):U^*U=UU^*=I_2\}$, where $U^*$ is conjugate
transpose. For each $U\in U(2)$ define
$$D(T_U)=\{f\in H^2(0,L):(U-I_2)\Gamma_0f+i\ell(U+I_2)\Gamma_1f=0\},\qquad T_Uf=-D^2f.$$
Then $T_{\min}\subseteq T_U\subseteq T_{\max}$, each $T_U$ is self-adjoint,
and every self-adjoint realization between $T_{\min}$ and $T_{\max}$ equals
exactly one $T_U$. The reference length makes the value and scaled derivative
boundary vectors have the same units if the interval coordinate is assigned
units; in the dimensionless mathematical model they are numerical vectors.
items.proof_route: Integrate by parts for boundary symplectic form, prove trace surjectivity with cubic polynomials, classify maximal isotropic planes by Cayley boundary coordinates.

references.title: Gerald Teschl, Mathematical Methods in Quantum Mechanics, 1st edition 2009
references.locator: Section 9.1, Lagrange identity and regular endpoint realizations, printed pp.181–186

references.title: Ovidiu Costin, Functional Analysis and Elements of Resurgence Theory
references.locator: Section 11.3, von Neumann extension theorem, printed pp.82–83

references.title: Manuel Asorey, Alberto Ibort, and Giuseppe Marmo, Global Theory of Quantum Boundary Conditions and Topology Change
references.locator: Section 2, printed pp.4–6; Appendix A, printed pp.19–20, interval Laplacian and U(2) boundary data

items.strategy:
**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement and Facts & Assumptions.

1.1 Let $T$ be any linear operator with $T_{\min}\subseteq T\subseteq T_{\max}$.
For this proof write $\gamma_b f=(\Gamma_0f,\Gamma_1f)\in
\mathbb C^2\times\mathbb C^2$. This is the four-coordinate trace map of
[F1] with the last coordinate sign reversed, so it is onto and has kernel
$D(T_{\min})$. Its image $M:=\gamma_b(D(T))$ is a linear subspace. Since
$\ker\gamma_b=D(T_{\min})\subseteq D(T)$, every $f\in H^2$ whose trace lies
in $M$ differs from a member of $D(T)$ by an element of $D(T_{\min})$; thus
$D(T)=\gamma_b^{-1}(M)$. Conversely, every linear subspace $M$ gives such a
domain because $\gamma_b$ is onto. [A1, F1, construct]

1.2 Define
$B((a,b),(a',b'))=\langle b,a'\rangle-\langle a,b'\rangle$ and
$M^\omega=\{z:B(m,z)=0\text{ for every }m\in M\}$. By [F2], integration by
parts gives $T^*=T_{\gamma_b^{-1}(M^\omega)}$: indeed, since
$T_{\min}\subseteq T$, adjoint inclusion reversal puts $D(T^*)$ inside
$D(T_{\min}^*)=H^2$, and for $g\in H^2$ the adjoint identity for every
$f\in D(T)$ is exactly $B(\gamma_b f,\gamma_b g)=0$. Hence $T$ is self-adjoint
if and only if $M=M^\omega$. [A1, F1, F2, F3]

2.1 Put $\gamma_\ell f=(a,b):=(\Gamma_0f,\ell\Gamma_1f)$ and let
$\widehat M=\gamma_\ell(D(T))$. Equivalently,
$\widehat M=\{(a,b):(a,b/\ell)\in M\}$, where $M$ is the unscaled trace
image from step 1.1. Define
$\widehat B((a,b),(a',b'))=\langle b,a'\rangle-\langle a,b'\rangle$ and
$\widehat M^{\widehat\omega}:=\{z:\widehat B(m,z)=0\text{ for all }m\in
\widehat M\}$.
Since $\widehat B=\ell B$ after undoing the derivative scaling and
$\ell>0$, step 1.2 gives $\widehat M=\widehat M^{\widehat\omega}$ exactly
when $T$ is self-adjoint. The map $\gamma_\ell$ is onto because the trace map
in [F1] is onto and multiplying its derivative coordinates by $\ell>0$ is
invertible. For $x=a+ib$ and $y=a-ib$, direct expansion using
the first-variable-linear inner product gives
$$\widehat B((a,b),(a',b'))=\frac{\langle x,x'\rangle-\langle y,y'\rangle}{2i}.$$
Thus $\widehat M=\widehat M^{\widehat\omega}$ implies that
$(a,b)\mapsto(x,y)$ sends $\widehat M$ to the graph of an
inner-product-preserving linear map $R:X\to\mathbb C^2$, where
$X=\{a+ib:(a,b)\in\widehat M\}$. It is well defined: if a member of
$\widehat M$ has $x=0$, isotropy gives $\|y\|^2=\|x\|^2=0$, so $y=0$.
Maximality forces
$X=\mathbb C^2$: otherwise choose $0\ne x_0\in X^\perp$ and take
$a=x_0/2$, $b=x_0/(2i)$, so $(x,y)=(x_0,0)$. The displayed identity makes
this boundary pair orthogonal for $\widehat B$ to all of $\widehat M$, hence it
lies in $\widehat M^{\widehat\omega}=\widehat M$; then
$x_0\in X\cap X^\perp$, a contradiction. Therefore
$R$ is an isometry from $\mathbb C^2$ into $\mathbb C^2$ and is onto because
both spaces have dimension two. It is a unitary matrix $U$, and its graph
condition is $U(a+ib)=a-ib$, equivalently
$(U-I_2)a+i(U+I_2)b=0$. This $U$ is unique because its value is fixed for
every $x\in\mathbb C^2$. [A1, F1, F2, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Conversely, let $U\in U(2)$ and set
$\widehat M_U=\{(a,b):U(a+ib)=a-ib\}$ in the scaled boundary coordinates.
Every $x\in\mathbb C^2$ occurs, by taking
$a=(x+Ux)/2$ and $b=(x-Ux)/(2i)$. Unitarity gives
$\langle x,x'\rangle=\langle Ux,Ux'\rangle$ for every pair, so the
displayed formula in step 2.1 makes $\widehat M_U$ isotropic. If
$(a,b)\in\widehat M_U^{\widehat\omega}$,
then for every $x'\in\mathbb C^2$ that formula gives
$\langle x',x\rangle=\langle Ux',y\rangle=\langle x',U^*y\rangle$, hence
$x=U^*y$ and $y=Ux$; therefore $(a,b)\in\widehat M_U$. Thus
$\widehat M_U=\widehat M_U^{\widehat\omega}$. Since $\gamma_\ell$ is onto,
the restriction to $\gamma_\ell^{-1}(\widehat M_U)$ is self-adjoint by the
criterion in step 1.2 and the scaling equivalence in step 2.1. Its boundary equation is exactly
the Statement's equation, and its domain lies between $T_{\min}$ and
$T_{\max}$ because it is a restriction of $T_{\max}$ whose domain contains
the zero-trace domain. [step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The preceding steps give a bijection from $U(2)$ to the entire set of
self-adjoint extensions between $T_{\min}$ and $T_{\max}$. By [F4], that same
extension set is uniquely parameterized by the abstract unitaries between
the deficiency subspaces. Composing the two bijections identifies the
boundary-matrix labels with the abstract deficiency labels and proves that
the displayed boundary family is exhaustive. [A1, F4, F5, step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎

items.title: A symmetric half-line momentum with no self-adjoint extension
items.design_state: Assigned design item; complete current statement and argument are recorded in its item carrier.
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice, Countable Choice, and Dependent Choice. On
$H=L^2(0,\infty;\mathbb C)$ let $S_c f=-iDf$ with domain
$D(S_c)=C_c^\infty(0,\infty)$. Its closure $\overline S_c$ has deficiency
indices $(n_+,n_-)=(1,0)$ at reference scale $E_*=1$, and therefore has no
self-adjoint extension on $H$.
items.proof_route: Adjoint is maximal H¹; solve f′=∓f and test L² at infinity; use deficiency parameterization.

items.strategy:
**Given:** The hypotheses of the Statement.

1.1 By [F5], the test functions are dense in $L^2(0,\infty)$. For
$f,g\in C_c^\infty(0,\infty)$, integration by parts [F1] gives
$\langle S_cf,g\rangle=\langle f,S_cg\rangle$ with no endpoint terms.
Thus $S_c$ is symmetric, so it is closable by [F2], and
$\overline S_c^{\,*}=S_c^*$. [A1, F1, F2, F5]

2.1 If $g\in H^1(0,\infty)$, [F1] gives
$\langle S_cf,g\rangle=\langle f,-iDg\rangle$ for every test $f$, so
$g\in D(S_c^*)$ and $S_c^*g=-iDg$. Conversely, if $g\in D(S_c^*)$ and
$h=S_c^*g$, testing the adjoint identity against every
$f\in C_c^\infty(0,\infty)$ says distributionally $Dg=i h\in L^2$.
Together with $g\in L^2$ this is exactly $g\in H^1$. Hence
$D(S_c^*)=H^1(0,\infty)$ and $S_c^*=-iD$. [A1, F1, F2, step 1.1]

3.1 By step 2.1, $g\in N_+(\overline S_c;1)$ exactly when
$g\in H^1$ and $-iDg=ig$, that is, $Dg=-g$. Its absolutely continuous
representative satisfies
$(e^xg(x))'=e^x(g(x)+g'(x))=0$ almost everywhere by the product rule in
[F3] and $g'=-g$. On each bounded subinterval the absolutely continuous
fundamental theorem in [F3] makes $e^xg(x)$ constant; overlap consistency
makes it one constant $c$ on the whole half-line. Thus $g(x)=ce^{-x}$. Since
$\int_0^\infty e^{-2x}\,dx=1/2$, this is in $L^2$ for every $c$, and
its classical derivative $-ce^{-x}$ is also in $L^2$ and is its weak
derivative by [F1]. Thus every such function is
in $H^1$ and satisfies the kernel equation, so
$N_+=\{ce^{-x}:c\in\mathbb C\}$ is one-dimensional. [A1, F1, F3, step 2.1, algebra]

3.2 A vector $g\in N_-(\overline S_c;1)$ satisfies $Dg=g$ by step 2.1, so
$(e^{-x}g(x))'=e^{-x}(g'(x)-g(x))=0$ almost everywhere by [F3] and
$g'=g$. On each bounded subinterval the absolutely continuous fundamental
theorem in [F3] makes $e^{-x}g(x)$ constant; overlap consistency gives
one $c\in\mathbb C$ on the whole half-line, so $g(x)=ce^x$. If $c\ne0$,
$\int_0^R|ce^x|^2dx=|c|^2(e^{2R}-1)/2\to\infty$, contradicting
$g\in L^2(0,\infty)$. Hence $c=0$, $N_- =\{0\}$ and $n_-=0$.
Combining step 3.1's positive-deficiency calculation with this result and the
common adjoint from step 1.1 gives the closure's indices $(1,0)$.
[A1, F1, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

4.1 The indices are unequal, so [F4] implies that $\overline S_c$ has no
self-adjoint extension on $H$. This proves the Statement.
[A1, F4, step 3.1, step 3.2] ∎

title: Operator domains, deficiency spaces and boundary realizations — Examples

items.title: Twisted circle momentum and its interval boundary matrix
items.design_state: Assigned design item; complete current statement and argument are recorded in its item carrier.
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice, Countable Choice, and Dependent Choice. Let
$L>0$, $\theta\in[0,2\pi)$, and $\hbar>0$. On $L^2(0,L;\mathbb C)$ let
$P_\theta f=-i\hbar Df$ with
$D(P_\theta)=\{f\in H^1(0,L):f(L)=e^{i\theta}f(0)\}$, using the continuous
Sobolev trace. Then $P_\theta$ is self-adjoint and has the complete
orthonormal eigenfamily
$$\phi_n(x)=L^{-1/2}e^{i(2\pi n+\theta)x/L},\qquad n\in\mathbb Z,$$
with eigenvalues $\hbar(2\pi n+\theta)/L$. Its squared realization
$P_\theta^2/\hbar^2$ is the interval Laplacian with domain
$\{f\in H^2(0,L):f(L)=e^{i\theta}f(0),\
f'(L)=e^{i\theta}f'(0)\}$. In the boundary convention of the A-page theorem,
this is the parameter
$$U_\theta=\begin{pmatrix}0&e^{-i\theta}\\e^{i\theta}&0\end{pmatrix}\in U(2).$$
items.proof_route: Fourier shift by e^{iθx/L} gives unitary equivalence to periodic Fourier multiplier.

items.strategy:
**Given:** The model operators and boundary conventions above.

1.1 The first supplier [F1] gives $P_\theta^0$ self-adjoint with the stated
eigenfamily and eigenvalues. Since $\hbar$ is a positive real scalar,
$P_\theta=\hbar P_\theta^0$ has the same domain and is self-adjoint: the
adjoint identity [F4] gives
$(\hbar P_\theta^0)^*=\hbar(P_\theta^0)^*$.
Moreover $P_\theta\phi_n=\hbar(2\pi n+\theta)\phi_n/L$, so the same complete
orthonormal family has the scaled eigenvalues in the Statement. [F1, F4, given, algebra]

1.2 By [F5], $f\in D(P_\theta^2)$ exactly when
$f\in D(P_\theta)$ and $P_\theta f\in D(P_\theta)$. The latter condition
requires $Df\in H^1$, hence $f\in H^2$ by [F3], and its twisted trace is
$-i\hbar f'(L)=e^{i\theta}(-i\hbar f'(0))$, equivalently
$f'(L)=e^{i\theta}f'(0)$. Thus $D(P_\theta^2)$ is exactly the stated
second-order domain, and $P_\theta^2/\hbar^2=-D^2$ there. [F1, F3, F5, algebra]

2.1 For a function in this domain write $c=f(0)$ and $d=f'(0)$. Its boundary
vectors are $a=c\,p$ and $b=\ell d\,q$, where
$p=(1,e^{i\theta})$ and $q=(1,-e^{i\theta})$. These vectors are orthogonal
and have equal norm, since $\langle p,q\rangle=1-e^{i\theta}e^{-i\theta}=0$
and $\|p\|^2=\|q\|^2=2$. The columns of the displayed matrix
$U_\theta$ are $(0,e^{i\theta})$ and $(e^{-i\theta},0)$, which are
orthonormal, so $U_\theta\in U(2)$. It sends $p$ to $p$ and $q$ to $-q$,
so for $x=a+ib=c\,p+i\ell d\,q$ it gives
$U_\theta x=c\,p-i\ell d\,q=a-ib$. Therefore
$(U_\theta-I_2)a+i(U_\theta+I_2)b=0$. Conversely, for any $f\in H^2(0,L)$
satisfying this equation, expand its boundary vectors as
$a=\alpha p+\beta q$ and $b=\gamma p+\delta q$; the orthogonal nonzero
vectors $p,q$ form a basis of $\mathbb C^2$. The equation becomes
$-2\beta q+2i\gamma p=0$, so $\beta=\gamma=0$. Hence
$f(L)=e^{i\theta}f(0)$ and, since $\ell>0$,
$f'(L)=e^{i\theta}f'(0)$. By [F2], this is exactly the
self-adjoint boundary realization $T_{U_\theta}$, which has the same domain
and action as $P_\theta^2/\hbar^2$. [F2, given, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

items.title: A symmetric operator need not have a self-adjoint extension
items.design_state: Assigned design item; complete current statement and argument are recorded in its item carrier.
items.statement: Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space and let $T:D(T)\to H$ be a densely defined symmetric linear operator. The false assertion is that there is a self-adjoint operator $A:D(A)\to H$ on the same Hilbert space with $D(T)\subseteq D(A)$ and $Af=Tf$ for every $f\in D(T)$. By Stone's theorem, such an $A$ would generate a strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group $U(t)=e^{itA}$ on $H$.
items.proof_route: Use the proved unequal deficiency indices.

items.strategy:
**Given:** Let $S_c=-iD$ on $C_c^\infty(0,\infty)$, with values in
$L^2(0,\infty;\mathbb C)$.

1.1 By [F2], for all test functions $f,g$,
$\langle S_cf,g\rangle=\langle f,S_cg\rangle$; thus the test-domain
operator is symmetric. [A1, F2]

1.2 The same operator's closure has unequal deficiency indices $(1,0)$, so
by [F1] it has no self-adjoint extension on the same Hilbert space. Thus
symmetry on the core does not guarantee a self-adjoint realization. [A1, F1]

2.1 If a strongly continuous unitary one-parameter group had a self-adjoint
generator $T$ extending $S_c$, Stone's theorem [F3] supplies that
self-adjointness. By [F4], $T$ is closed and contains the least closed
extension $\overline S_c$: explicitly, every point of the graph of
$\overline S_c$ is a limit of graph points of $S_c$, and the closed graph of
$T$ contains each such limit. This contradicts [F1], which says
$\overline S_c$ has no self-adjoint extension. Thus the proposed general
claim fails for this operator while its integration-by-parts symmetry
hypothesis holds. [A1, F1, F3, F4, step 1.2] ∎
